General Chiang forced his hand in expectation of destroying all Japanese
boats in the Whangpoo and wiping out the small Japanese garrison. The
Chinese no doubt placed a great deal more confidence in their Air Force
then subsequent events have justified.
It is true of course that the Chines e
Air Force should have blown every Japanese boat out of the Whengpoo during
the first two or three days of the conflict and should also have prevented
the landing of troops at Woosung or for that matter even the approach of
airplane carriers or transports.
So far as your comment upon the Japanese action at Shanghai is
concerned in spite of what you say to the contrary,
there was no real need
for the Japanese to take Shanghai as it would have been very simple for the
Japanese to have stopped all ships at the entrance to the Yangtsze and thus
have blocked Shanghai as effectively as they have blocked Canton or Tsingtag
for instance, at neither of which places have they landed any troops.
I note your opinion that the wer will be long drawn out provided
China can get the necessary supplies.
It is true as you point out that there
is no gasoline produced in China but large quantities have been shipped in
through Hongkong and when this source of supply is eliminated through des-
truction of the Canton Kowloon Railroad then the Chinese will have to rely
for a gasoline supply on the highway from Russia running to Urumohi, Hami
and Lanchow and on the overland routes from Yunnenfu, which place is in turn
served as you know by the railroad to Hanoi.
It is extremely unlikely in
my opinion that the Japanese will be able to put that railroad out of com-
mission as it is too far removed from any base the Japanese are likely to
estanlish on the south China cosst.
